newsitem.title: UK: U.S warns of dangers of C.European reform stalling.
newsitem.headline: U.S warns of dangers of C.European reform stalling.

text.p: Events in southern central Europe over the last year show that if economic reforms collapse the effects can be dire, a U.S. treasury official told the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development on Monday.

"In the southern tier (of central European countries), the last 12 months offer a sober warning: the price of stalled or abandoned reforms can be far worse than stagnation," assistant director to the U.S. treasury David Lipton told the EBRD's annual meeting.
He pointed out the relevance of the EBRD to Albania, which he said had been pushed to the edge of anarchy by inadequate financial regulation.

Lipton said the northern group of countries had made considerable progress on liberalisation, stabilisation and privatisation but more intensive structural and sectoral reform measures were now needed to increase and sustain growth.
In the south, Bulgaria and Romania were now poised to restart reform amid new political opportunities.
"These two countries have a historic opportunity to press ahead with reform and offer real hope to their people," Lipton said, adding that Bosnia was also nearing a key decision point.

"The true test of the Dayton Accord will be whether the three parties can agree to participate jointly in economic institutions and policy making to begin to rebuild their country," he said, referring to the U.S.-brokered peace accord that ended the 1992-95 war in Bosnia.
Lipton said that Russia's efforts to tackle the second stage of structural reforms needed to be supported but warned that Ukraine was in danger of missing the chance to reform decisively.

"If the (Ukranian) authorities do not move forward with the package of fiscal and regulatory reform, it could be some time before there is so promising an opportunity," he said. Lipton also highlighted the Caspian region where "the extraordinary natural wealth is drawing the attention of foreign private capital" but this wealth risked remaining untapped if obstacles to investment were not overcome.

The U.S. official joined others at the meeting in voicing his concern over crime and corruption in the former Soviet Union and eastern bloc countries. "Good performance depends on an open and transparent society in which citizens' voices are heard, in both politics and business," he said.
Transparency was a powerful weapon in fighting crime and corruption, both factors which undermined legal and regulatory regimes and discouraged long-term investment.

Deregulation would reduce the opportunities for favourtism and corruption but this needed to be backed up by clear statements from political leaders and prosecutions to demonstrate that no one was above the law, he added.
